title: The hand on the rock
hookLine: tradition says that at Hasan Abdal a boulder rolled down at him stopped at his open palm

lines: A HOT DAY NEAR HASAN ABDAL.
MARDANA ASKS FOR WATER, THREE TIMES.
cards: A hot day in the hills of what's now northern Pakistan, near a town called Hasan Abdal. Two travelers have been walking a long time, and one of them, Mardana, is desperately thirsty. There's no water below.
But at the top of the hill, tradition says, lives a holy man named Wali Qandhari, and he has a spring. So Mardana climbs up and asks for a drink. He's turned away.
Nanak sends him back up to ask again. Turned away again. A third time: nothing.
A cup of water is about the smallest thing one traveler can ask of another, and three times the answer is no.

teach.h: WATER RISES AT THE FOOT OF THE HILL.
teach.b: Nanak, tradition says, told Mardana to lift a stone at the foot of the hill. Water came up from underneath, clear and cold. At the top, Wali Qandhari's spring began to fail.
Furious, he pushed a huge boulder down the hillside toward the two men. Nanak didn't run.

teach.h: A BOULDER ROLLS; AN OPEN PALM.
teach.b: He raised one hand, palm open, and the rock stopped against it. When it settled, the story says, the shape of his hand was pressed into the stone. That handprint named the place.

teach.h: PANJA SAHIB — THE PLACE OF THE PALM.
teach.b: Panja means the palm of the hand, and the gurdwara there, Panja Sahib, keeps a stone with a handprint that pilgrims still touch, with water running beneath it. Sikh pilgrims still cross the border to visit it.
How do Sikhs hold a story like this? Like the milk and blood, in more than one way. Some hold it as a miracle.

teach.h: NOT A FIST: AN OPEN, STEADY HAND.
teach.b: Others read it as a picture of something every life needs: a hand that stays steady when something heavy comes rolling at you.

The story comes from later tradition, not the scripture, and people remember Wali Qandhari differently: a shrine to him still stands on that hilltop. So the rock is the center of the story, not the man who pushed it.
Watch the hand. It doesn't push back. It doesn't strike.
A steady hand isn't a fist.

how: Sikh pilgrims visit Gurdwara Panja Sahib at Hasan Abdal, in Pakistan, where they touch the handprint in the stone and bathe in the spring.

games.q: you're at the bottom of the hill. a boulder is rolling straight at you. what does Nanak do?
o: shout at the man who pushed it.
games.why: tradition says he raised an open hand and the rock stopped against it, leaving the print of his palm.

practice: Stand close to a wall, a door, or a tree if you're outside, and press your palm flat against it, not hard, just enough to feel it press back. Breathe, and let your arm be strong without being tense.
Think of one heavy thing rolling toward you this week, and let your hand stay open.

wordCard.voice: Panja. The palm, the word behind Panja Sahib, the shrine built where tradition says Guru Nanak's open hand stopped a boulder at Hasan Abdal.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: panja, the palm with five fingers spread; Panja Sahib is named for the handprint.
